Vs.

full_judgment:
Facts material for the appeal are that dispute between plaintiff-appellant, Golan Hafez Mia, and defendant respondent, Khadem Ali Meah centres round the land belonging to Nalini and his wife Sarala. They left the country for West Bengal in 1962. Their rayati holding fell in arrears of rent which prompted the Government Acquired Estate to start four certificate proceedings. They are certificate case Nos. 138/1961-62, 185/1961-62, 187/1961-62, and 1970/1962-63. The holding comprising 1.72 acres of land was sold on 22-19-1962. It was purchased by the plaintiff, and he took delivery of possession on 4-10-62, Dispute between two parties cropped up when plain-tiff who had mututed his name in the Government Acquired Estate, found that the defendant on the basis of an ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 730/62, had got his name entered in the record of rights. Defendant got the ex-party decree, as his name was omitted from the record of rights. His claim is that in Baishak 1350 B.S. corresponding to April 1973, he got settlement of the land from Nalini and Sarala, on the basis of Lakhik and has been in possession since then. The suit of the plaintiff was for declaration only. The suit was contested on various grounds; one was that the plaintiff did not acquire a valid title in the certificate sale, and the other was that he was not in possession of the property. 

 5. Of the two points, we propose to deal with the second question first. Before entering into the construction of the section, the finding of the High Court is to be looked into in order to ascertain the fact in its proper context. Both the plaintiff and the defendant claim title from Nalini and his wife. The plaintiff's claim is that by virtue of his auction purchase, Nalini's title was extinguished and vested in him. The defendant's claim is that long before the certificate sale, he in 1943 took settlement of the land, and is in possession of it, and so his title has not been affected by the certificate purchase of the plaintiff. The Courts below have concurrently found that the defendant has failed to substantiate his acquisition of title on the footing of settlement, and that the ex-parte decree obtained by him was fraudulent and void. This finding was not in challenge before the High Court. On the acceptance of this concurrent finding as to defendant's title, the observation of the High Court regarding plaintiff's title on the interpretation of section 20 of the Act seems to be out of place. The question before the High Court was what title was acquired by the plaintiff in the certificate sale. And having found that the defendant was on the land without any title, the High Court was in error in going to the question of title acquired by the plaintiff under section 20 of the Act, because defendant's claim of title through the certificate debtors had failed. But the defendant being in possession, the question to be determined is, whether plaintiff has a better title to recover possession from him. 

 6. Since leave has been granted to consider the question, we propose to deal with it, in the proper perspective. We first propose to deal with relevant provisions of the Act, and see what title an auction purchaser acquires in a certificate sale, in terms of the provisions of the Act, and whether the finding of the High Court on the imperfect acquisition of title by the plaintiff, is correct. We also propose to deal with some of the rulings of the Dacca High Court on the question which requires restatement. To understand what title is acquired on a certificate sale some of the salient provisions of the Act are to be looked into. 

 10. We now turn to sections 20 and 36 to see what consequence follow after the sale in execution of a certificate. Section 20 consists of 4 sub-sections. We are concerned with two of them, sub-sections (1) and (3), and other two sub-sections are not material for our consideration. Sub-section (1) says, that when a property is sold in execution of a certificate, there shall vest in the purchaser merely the right, title and interest of the certificate debtor at the time of the sale, even though the property itself be specified. Sub-section (3) is an exception to sub-section (1), and it begins with a non obstante clause. The relevant part says: notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), or any other law for the time being in force where the tenure or holding is sold in execution of a certificate, for arrears of rent due in respect thereof, the tenure or holding, shall, subject to the provisions of section 90 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, where that section is in force, pass to the purchaser with the power to annul encumbrances with the restriction provided by the Act. This is the material part of the section relevant for our purposes excluding the immaterial portions. 

 11. The substance of the two sub-sections may be considered by drawing an analogy from the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act, in that the effect of the sale in execution of a certificate under sub-section (1), is that of a money decree, and that under sub-section (3) of a rent decree in certain cases. Under the former, the right title and interest of the certificate-debtor on the date of sale, and under the latter the tenure or holding will pass to the purchaser with the right to annul the encumbrances. Ordinarily the right title and interest of the certificate-debtor at the time of the sale vest in the purchaser. He steps into the shoes of the certificate debtor, and claims through him. All lawful liabilities created on the and by the certificate debtor before period of the service of notice under section 7, or the attachment, will bind the purchaser. If the certificate debtor had no subsisting interest on the date of the sale it is a nullity. These are the incident of a money-decree. 

 13. Turning to the facts of the present case, we find that the certificate proceeding was initiated for the realization of arrears of rent, due to the Government Acquired Estate from Nalini and his wife. The consequences of the certificate proceeding therefore came under sub-section (3) of section 20. The plaintiff purchaser acquired a paramount title in the certificate sale. The certificate sale under sub-section (3), we have already observed, corresponds to rent decree in some cases, and the purchaser acquires an absolute title in the holding, except the protected interest described in the proviso to the sub-section (3), but with the right to annul the encumbrances in the manner prescribed under the Act. We are not concerned with any protected interest here. The defendant, no doubt claimed an under rayati right by virtue of a settlement from Nalini and his wife, the certificate debtors. But his claim has not succeeded, On the contrary, the ex-parte decree obtained by him in Title suit No. 730/62 on the basis of his settlement, has been found by the Courts below to be fraudulent and void, The defendant, therefore, has been found bereft of any legal title, or interest capable of protection under sub-section (3) of section 20. The High Court was in error in not looking at the true character of the certificate sale, and erroneously proceeded solely on the basis of sub-section (1) of section 20 of the Act, ignoring sub-section (3). Even under sub-section (1) the purchaser, as in a money decree, acquires the right, title and interest of the certificate debtor on date of the sale. The defendant however claimed a subordinate interest under the certificate debtors, but his claim was negatived by the courts below, His claim does not stand under any of the two sub-sections The concurrent findings of the two courts are that the defendant acquired no valid title in the certificate land, The certificate debtors being the sole tenants, and the plaintiff the sole purchaser of the certificate sale, he, under S. 20 (1) of the Act acquired the right, title and interest of the certificate-debtors, and in the present case the entire interest in the holdings in question, and the holdings also passed to the plaintiff under section 20(3) with right to annul the encumbrances. 

 19. We now propose to consider some of the decisions of the Dacca High Court, cited before us which require reconsideration of some of the legal propositions stated therein. First we take the case of Mohammad Moslem Ali Molla vs. Sk. Azaharali, P.L.R. 1957 Dacca 6, a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court. In that case, the dispute arose over a town property in the Dacca City situated at Bonogram lane. The plaintiff claimed the property on the basis of purchase from the certificate debtor, Kamini Kumar Mazumdar by a registered kabala dated March 23, 1952. The defendant resisted the claim, on the footing of purchase of properly in a certificate sale, held on 10th July, 1952. It is to be noted that the plaintiff purchased the properly after notice under section 7 of Act was said to have been served on June 6, 1951. The question principally turned on the voidness of the purchase of the plaintiff in terms of S. 8 of the Act. Incidentally section 36, and other sections of the Act were considered. Another question was the maintainability of the suit under section 37 of the Act. The High Court on evidence, held that there was fraud before, and after the sale, and so the title was found in favour of the private purchaser, the plaintiff. The conclusion of the High Court on the facts found by it, cannot be taken exception to, but while dealing with the question of non-service of notice under section 7 of the Act, an observation has been made, that rule 6(b) cannot be resorted to for service of notice under S. 7, and that the service of notice under rule 6(b) is non-service in the eye of law. We think, that this statement of law as to the interpretation of section 7, on the question of service of notice, is not sound. Section 7 says that when a certificate has been filed, a certificate officer, shall cause to be served upon the certificate debtor, in the prescribed manner, a notice in the prescribed form. The prescribed manner is to be found in rule 2 to 9 contained in Schedule II of the Act. A reading of the rules shows, that there must be an attempt to serve the notice directly on the certificate debtor in person. But there is also the alternative provision for service, by way of substituted service, if the attempt at personal service fails. That is contained in rule 6(a) and (b). It is to be observed that clauses (a) and (b) have been so worded; as to make them alternative subordinate clauses of the principal clause, embodied in rule 6, so that when the condition of the principal clause of rule 6 is satisfied, then one of the alternate clauses (a) or (b) can be resorted to, if the requirement of the alternative clauses, is fulfilled. Both the clauses prescribe the different modes of substituted service, For the application of rule 6(b), all that is necessary, is that, if there be land affected by the notice, alternative method of service under this clause can be resorted to. It is further to be remembered, that for the sale of immovable property affected by the certificate, specific rules have been provided in rules 23 and 46. It is also to be noted that in terms of section 8, immediately on the service of notice under section 7, transfer of immovable property of the certificate debtor within the district where certificate is filed, is prohibited amounting to an attachment of the properties ; and all his properties, wherever situated, are charged with certificate dues. In this view of the matter, so much of the decision in Mohammad Moslemali Molla's case which says, that rule 6(b) cannot be resorted to for service under section 7 of the Act, is not correct. For substituted service of notice under section 7 of the Act, both the alternate clauses (a) and (b) of rule 6 can be resorted to, according to the facts of each case. 

 20. The other decision of the Dacca High Court, which calls for attention, is a decision of 4 single Judge in the case of Tarangini Devi vs. Govinda Mallik 9 D.L.R. 57. The decision arose out of a suit for setting aside the certificate sale, and the plaintiff claiming that her interest in the certificate sale had not been affected. A question arose, whether non-service of notice under section 7 makes the certificate sale a nullity. The learned Judge referred to the case of Puma Chandra vs. Dinabandha Mukherjee I.L.R. 34 Cal. 811, a decision of a Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court, and held that the non-service of notice under section 7, renders the certificate sale a nullity. It is to be noticed, that another Single Bench of the Dacca High Court, in the case of Abtabur Rahman vs. Madan Mia 19 D.L.R. 333. has not only taken a contrary view, but has dissented from the view taken in Tarangini Devi and held that non-service of notice under section 7, does not render the sale a nullity. We find that the Single Judge in Tarangini Devi, following the authority of Purna Chandra, held the sale to be a nullity because of non-service of notice. We have already referred to the legislative interference to settle the conflicting judicial decisions on this question. In Purna Chanda's case an observation of the Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court, is there calling for legislation, not only to resolve the conflict of decisions, but also to protect the auction purchaser from undue harassment and to safeguard his auction purchase. We have already given our interpretation to S. 36. We therefore find that Tarangini Devi 19 D.L.R, 57 is not a correct statement of law, whereas in Abtabur Rahman a correct view has been taken, in that non-service of notice does not render the sale a nullity. It is a valid sale unless set aside in the manner and within the recede prescribed by section 36. 

 21. We may now turn to the facts of the present case. The Trial Court has held that the notice under section 7, was not served personally upon the certificate debtor, but it was served on the land under rule 6(b), and such service is no service of notice at all, The Court of appeal below affirmed this finding, following the case of Tarangini Devi, and held that, it was a case of non-service and so the sale was void. It appears that the certificate proceeding was started by the Government Acquired Estate, for realisation of arreas of rent. Section 20(3) of the Act says, that when a proceeding under the Act, is taken for execution of a certificate for arrears of rent, the tenure or holding is to be sold, which means that the land is affected by the notice, and therefore, rule 6(b) can be resorted to, if personal service has failed. The order sheet of the certificate proceeding clearly shows that personal service of notice under section 7 of the Act had failed, and thereafter service of notice under rule 46 read with rule 6 (b) was resorted to. The Courts below were in error in not regarding this service as good service under section 7 of the Act. The learned Judges of the Dacca High Court, upon the facts found by the Courts below held that it was a case of non-service of notice, which makes a sale not void but voidable. The High Court committed a second error in so finding because two reasons: first, validity of a certificate sale cannot be challenged on the ground of non-service of notice under S. 7 by way of defence, and secondly, even if there has been non-service of notice, the certificate sale is valid, unless it set aside in the prescribed manner and within the period contained in S. 36 of the Act. Apart from the two grounds, the High Court perpetuated the error of the Courts below in treating the substituted service under rules 6 (b) as non-service. 

 24. In the result the appeal is allowed. with the above finding, the decisions of the courts below are set aside in part, and the case remitted back to trial Court for allowing the plaintiff- appellant to amend his pleading, by adding the prayer for recovery of possession on payment of proper court fees. The defendant shall be at liberty to file additional written statement, the court below shall decide the question of the recovery of possession by the plaintiff, and the ancillary question of adverse possession of the defendant, if so raised. The question will be decided on the evidence on record. The court shall, however, be at liberty to allow such additional evidence, if the parties pray and the court thinks fit to allow. The prayer for amendment if not made within three weeks of the arrival of the records in the court below, the shall be dismissed with cost. The cost of this appeal shall abide the result of the suit.
